title: Anomalous Microwave Response in YBCO Resonators beyond the Two-Level-System Model
authors: Kaiwen Zheng, Nathan J. Johnson, Nathan T. Thobaben, Sidharth Duthaluru, Haochen Shen, Denae T. Cherry, David S. Wisbey, Kater W. Murch
abstract: We report the microwave response of coplanar-waveguide (CPW) resonators fabricated from $\mathrm{YBa_2Cu_3O_{7-δ}}$ (YBCO) thin films over temperatures from approximately $70~\mathrm{mK}$ to $40~\mathrm{K}$. The resonators exhibit internal quality factors $Q_\mathrm{i}$ in the range of $4\times10^3$ to $10^4$ at 70 mK, which increase to a maximum of approximately $8\times10^3$ to $1.2\times10^4$ near $6~\mathrm{K}$. At low temperatures, both $Q_\mathrm{i}$ and the fractional shift of the resonance frequency $Δf_\mathrm{r}/f_\mathrm{r}$ increases with temperature, qualitatively resembling behavior commonly associated with two-level-system (TLS) defects. However, neither response saturates on the temperature scale set by the resonator frequency, and the loss exhibits no observable microwave-power dependence. We show that low-temperature frequency upturn may be better described by an additional paramagnetic response associated with defect-induced local moments or Andreev bound states, while the low-temperature loss follows an approximately logarithmic temperature dependence whose microscopic origin remains unresolved. These measurements establish the millikelvin performance of patterned YBCO resonators and show that their low-temperature response cannot be understood within the conventional TLS framework alone.
summary: The authors measured the microwave response of YBCO resonators at very low temperatures to study superconducting dissipation. They found that while some behavior resembles Two-Level Systems, the data requires an additional paramagnetic contribution for frequency shifts and exhibits a residual loss following a logarithmic temperature dependence. This suggests that the underlying physics is more complex than standard TLS models predict.
main_problem: The study aims to characterize the anomalous microwave response of YBCO resonators at low temperatures, specifically demonstrating that conventional Two-Level-System (TLS) models fail to explain the observed frequency shift and loss.
main_result: The low-temperature frequency upturn is better described by an additional paramagnetic contribution from local moments or Andreev bound states, while the residual loss follows a logarithmic temperature dependence with an unknown microscopic origin.
method: Microwave characterization of coplanar-waveguide (CPW) resonators fabricated from YBCO thin films, measuring intrinsic quality factor ($Q_i$) and resonance frequency shift ($\Delta f_r/f_r$) across temperatures from 70 mK to 40 K.
model_or_system: The physical system is a superconducting film (YBCO) patterned into CPW resonators. The analysis compares experimental data against theoretical models, including the Two-Level-System (TLS) model and paramagnetic response models derived from local moments or Andreev bound states.
key_observables: Intrinsic quality factor ($Q_i$), fractional resonance frequency shift ($\Delta f_r/f_r$), microwave power dependence of $Q_i$, and temperature dependence of loss.
important_parameters: Temperature range (70 mK to 40 K), characteristic energy scales related to the resonator frequency, and fit parameters describing paramagnetic or TLS contributions.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the observed low-temperature behavior can be modeled by combining quasiparticle loss with either a TLS contribution or a paramagnetic contribution; however, it notes limitations in these assumptions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate resonator layouts and $|S_{21}|$ measurements. Key plots show temperature dependence of $Q_i$ and $\Delta f_r/f_r$, comparing fits from the standard TLS model against those incorporating paramagnetic or logarithmic dependencies.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by presenting microwave measurements across a wide temperature range, analyzing the data to rule out simple models (like pure TLS), proposing alternative physical mechanisms (paramagnetic response) for frequency shifts, and finally identifying an unresolved logarithmic loss channel.
why_interesting: This work directly probes superconducting gap physics and dissipation mechanisms in high-temperature superconductors, which are central topics in strongly correlated electron systems. The failure of standard models highlights the complexity of low-energy excitations near quantum critical points or disorder-induced states.
